seoDescription: Step-by-step guide to building a standards-compliant REST API with ASP.NET Core (2.2/3/5) covering project setup, cleaning MVC scaffolding, configuring DbContext and appsettings, installing and configuring Swagger (Swashbuckle), creating a test controller and endpoints, and wiring middleware and Swagger UI. Learn best practices for route templates, versioning groundwork, and minimal, secure API hosting configuration for production-ready services.

chapters.title: Introduction and goals
chapters.description: Overview of the tutorial goals: build a proper RESTful API in ASP.NET Core, follow REST architecture and patterns.

chapters.title: Create the project and initial template choices
chapters.description: Create a new ASP.NET Core web application, choose the MVC template to retain Identity for later, and name the project.

chapters.title: Remove unneeded MVC scaffolding and rename DbContext
chapters.description: Prune the default MVC files and folders, keep only what is necessary, and rename ApplicationDbContext to AppDbContext.

chapters.title: Switch hosting mode and trim startup
chapters.description: Remove IIS Express integration, set the app to run as an executable, and remove remaining MVC/UI pieces and Bootstrap references.

chapters.title: What is Swagger and create a test controller
chapters.description: Introduce Swagger as documentation and tooling, then add a simple TestController with a GET endpoint to prove the API runs.

chapters.title: Run the app, see JSON output, and install Swashbuckle
chapters.description: Run the project to confirm the endpoint returns JSON, then install the Swashbuckle.AspNetCore package to add Swagger functionality.

chapters.title: Configure Swagger options, middleware, services, and run
chapters.description: Create a SwaggerOptions configuration class, bind it in Startup, add UseSwagger and UseSwaggerUI middleware, configure SwaggerGen services, and verify the UI and API definition.

summary:
## Key Concepts

- **RESTful API vs JSON endpoints**
  - Returning JSON does not make an API RESTful; follow REST architectural constraints and standards.

- **Project template and Identity**
  - Use the **MVC template** initially to retain **individual user accounts** (Identity) for later use.
  - Prune unnecessary MVC scaffolding (Views, Models, HomeController) to minimize surface area for an API.

- **Hosting and environment**
  - Remove **IIS Express** integration to run as an executable when appropriate.
  - Keep minimal environment configuration necessary for testing and production.

- **Configuration organization**
  - Centralize API settings in **appsettings** and create option classes (e.g., **SwaggerOptions**) to bind configuration sections.
  - Use Configuration.GetSection("SectionName").Bind(...) to map JSON to strongly typed options.

- **Swagger (Swashbuckle)**
  - Install **Swashbuckle.AspNetCore** to provide Swagger generation and Swagger UI middleware.
  - Register middleware in Startup.Configure: **UseSwagger()** and **UseSwaggerUI(...)** with route templates and the Swagger endpoint.
  - Register generator in Startup.ConfigureServices: **services.AddSwaggerGen(c => c.SwaggerDoc("v1", new ...))** and set API title/version.
  - Swagger JSON and UI endpoints are environment-agnostic and can be configured via options.

- **Quick endpoint testing**
  - Create a simple controller with a GET action returning **IActionResult** and **Ok(object)** to verify JSON responses.
  - Use the Swagger UI to discover and exercise endpoints and confirm response codes and payloads.

> [!TIP] Create small, testable endpoints first to verify your middleware and configuration before adding domain logic.

> [!NOTE] Keep boilerplate configuration in option classes and configuration files so the same settings can be reused across environments.

> [!IMPORTANT] Configuring Swagger does not replace designing proper API routes or versioning strategy; plan route templates and API versioning in subsequent steps.
